title: Maxima and minima
summary: Critical points are where the derivative is zero or undefined. The second-derivative test classifies some of them, is silent when the second derivative is zero, and does not by itself give a global extremum.
intuition:
A local maximum is a point where the function is at least as large as the nearby values. A local minimum is the same idea with the inequality reversed. A global maximum is the greatest value on the whole domain under discussion, which may be larger than the set of nearby points. The second-derivative test only talks about the local question, and only at an interior critical point.

A critical point is a place where $f'(c)=0$ or where $f'(c)$ does not exist. Endpoints of a closed interval are checked when the problem asks for a global extremum, and they are not automatically called critical points. On the whole real line a local peak need not be global: $x^{3}-3x$ peaks at height $2$ near $x=-1$ and then tends to infinity.

The second-derivative test reads the concavity at a point where $f'(c)=0$. Positive means the graph opens upward, a local minimum. Negative means a local maximum. Zero means the test says nothing. Both $x^{3}$ and $x^{4}$ have a vanishing second derivative at the origin, and they behave differently: $x^{3}$ is neither a local max nor a local min, while $x^{4}$ has a local and global minimum.

$$f''(c)>0\Rightarrow \text{local min},\qquad f''(c)<0\Rightarrow \text{local max}.$$

definitions.body: An interior point $c$ of the domain is a critical point when $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist. Every local extremum in the interior occurs at a critical point. The converse is false: $x^{3}$ has a critical point at $0$ and no local extremum there.

$f(c)$ is a local maximum when $f(x)\leq f(c)$ for every $x$ in some open interval around $c$. It is a local minimum when $f(x)\geq f(c)$ on such an interval. The comparison is local, not against the whole domain.

A global maximum on a set $S$ is a value $f(c)$, with $c\in S$, such that $f(x)\leq f(c)$ for every $x\in S$. A local maximum need not be global. On $\mathbb{R}$, a cubic can have a local maximum and still be unbounded above.
Suppose $f'(c)=0$ and $f''(c)$ exists. If $f''(c)>0$, then $f$ has a local minimum at $c$. If $f''(c)<0$, then $f$ has a local maximum at $c$. If $f''(c)=0$, the test is silent.

formulas.name: Critical point
formulas.note: Interior local extrema occur among these points. Endpoints are extra candidates when the domain is a closed interval.

formulas.name: Second-derivative test
formulas.note: This needs $f'(c)=0$. The case $f''(c)=0$ says nothing: compare $x^{3}$ and $x^{4}$ at $0$.

formulas.name: First-derivative sign change
formulas.note: No sign change means the critical point is not a local extremum, as with $f'(x)=3x^{2}$ for $f(x)=x^{3}$.

properties: If $f'(c)=0$ and $f''(c)>0$, the critical point is a local minimum. If $f''(c)<0$, it is a local maximum. The test does not compare this local value with distant values or with endpoints.

If $f''(c)=0$, the second-derivative test is silent. For $f(x)=x^{3}$ at $0$ there is no local extremum. For $f(x)=x^{4}$ at $0$ there is a local minimum. The same vanishing second derivative covers both outcomes.
$f'(x)=3x^{2}-3$ for $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$, so the critical points are $x=\pm 1$. Then $f''(x)=6x$ gives a local maximum value $2$ at $x=-1$ and a local minimum value $-2$ at $x=1$.
Those local values are not global on $\mathbb{R}$. As $x\to\infty$, $x^{3}-3x\to\infty$, and as $x\to-\infty$ the function tends to $-\infty$.
A point where $f'$ does not exist can be a local extremum. The absolute value has a local minimum at $0$ even though the derivative there does not exist. It is still a critical point.

examples.title: Classify the critical points of a cubic
examples.prompt: Find and classify the critical points of $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Decide which local extrema are global.
steps: Differentiate: $f'(x)=3x^{2}-3=3(x^{2}-1)=3(x-1)(x+1)$. The derivative exists everywhere, so the critical points are the zeros $x=1$ and $x=-1$.
The second derivative is $f''(x)=6x$. At $x=1$, $f''(1)=6>0$, so $x=1$ is a local minimum. The value is $f(1)=1-3=-2$.
At $x=-1$, $f''(-1)=-6<0$, so $x=-1$ is a local maximum. The value is $f(-1)=-1+3=2$.

The function is a cubic with positive leading coefficient, so $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$ and $f(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$. The local maximum $2$ is not a global maximum, and the local minimum $-2$ is not a global minimum.
examples.answer: Local maximum value $2$ at $x=-1$, local minimum value $-2$ at $x=1$. Neither is global on $\mathbb{R}$.

examples.title: The second-derivative test goes silent
examples.prompt: Apply the second-derivative test to $f(x)=x^{3}$ and to $g(x)=x^{4}$ at $x=0$, and classify each point another way.
steps: For $f(x)=x^{3}$, $f'(x)=3x^{2}$ and $f''(x)=6x$. Both $f'(0)$ and $f''(0)$ are $0$. The second-derivative test says nothing.

The first derivative $3x^{2}$ does not change sign: it is nonnegative on both sides of $0$. Also $f(-0.1)=-0.001<0$ and $f(0.1)=0.001>0$, so every neighbourhood of $0$ contains values above $f(0)$ and values below $f(0)$. The origin is not a local extremum.
For $g(x)=x^{4}$, $g'(x)=4x^{3}$ and $g''(x)=12x^{2}$. Again $g'(0)=g''(0)=0$, so the second-derivative test says nothing.
But $g(x)=x^{4}\geq 0=g(0)$ for every real $x$. The origin is a local minimum and also the global minimum, even though $g''(0)=0$.
examples.answer: Both tests are silent at $0$. The function $x^{3}$ has neither a local max nor a local min there. The function $x^{4}$ has a local and global minimum there.

traps: Reading $f''(c)=0$ as 'not an extremum'. For $x^{4}$ at $0$ the second derivative vanishes and the point is a minimum. The test is silent, not negative.

Reading $f''(c)=0$ as 'an extremum of unknown type' and stopping. For $x^{3}$ at $0$ the second derivative vanishes and there is no local extremum at all. A sign chart or a direct comparison is required.
Promoting a local maximum to a global maximum. The value $2$ of $x^{3}-3x$ at $x=-1$ is only local; $f(3)=18$ is already larger.
Forgetting a critical point where the derivative does not exist. On a domain that includes $0$, $|x|$ has its minimum at a point where $f'$ is undefined.
python:
def f(x):
    return x ** 3 - 3 * x

assert f(1) == -2 and f(-1) == 2
assert 3 * (1) ** 2 - 3 == 0
assert 6 * 1 > 0 and 6 * (-1) < 0
assert (-0.1) ** 3 < 0 < (0.1) ** 3
assert all((k / 5) ** 4 >= 0 for k in range(-10, 11))

def wide(x):
    return x ** 3 - 12 * x

assert wide(-2) == 16 and wide(2) == -16
assert 3 * ((-2) ** 2) - 12 == 0
print(f(-1), f(1), wide(-2))

questions.stem: For $f(x)=x^{3}$ at $x=0$, the second-derivative test and the local behaviour say that
options: $f''(0)=0$, the test is silent, and $0$ is not a local extremum
$f''(0)=0$, the test is silent, and $0$ is a local minimum
questions.solution:
The answer is **C**.

$f'(x)=3x^{2}$ and $f''(x)=6x$, so $f'(0)=f''(0)=0$. The test gives no classification. Because $f$ takes both negative values, such as $f(-0.1)=-0.001$, and positive values, such as $f(0.1)=0.001$, the number $f(0)=0$ is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. Option D is the correct story for $x^{4}$, not for $x^{3}$.

questions.stem: For $g(x)=x^{4}$ at $x=0$, which statement is correct?
options: $g''(0)>0$, so the second-derivative test reports a local minimum
$g''(0)=0$, so the test is silent, but $g$ has a local minimum at $0$
$0$ is not a critical point of $g$
questions.solution:
The answer is **B**.

$g'(x)=4x^{3}$ is zero at $0$, so the origin is a critical point. $g''(x)=12x^{2}$ is also zero there, so the second-derivative test does not fire. Independently, $x^{4}\geq 0$ for every real $x$, with equality only at $0$, so the origin is a local minimum. A zero second derivative is not a report of a maximum, and it is not a positive second derivative.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$. Which of the following are true?
options: $f$ has a global maximum on $\mathbb{R}$ at $x=-1$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A and B**.

$f'(x)=3x^{2}-3=3(x-1)(x+1)$, so the only critical points are $x=\pm 1$. And $f''(x)=6x$, so $f''(1)=6>0$ and $x=1$ is a local minimum, with value $f(1)=-2$.

The local maximum at $x=-1$ has value $2$, but $f(3)=18>2$, so it is not global. At $x=0$, $f'(0)=-3\neq 0$ and the derivative exists, so $0$ is not a critical point.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: A critical point is a point where $f'$ is zero or $f'$ does not exist.
If $f'(c)=0$ and $f''(c)>0$, then $f$ has a local minimum at $c$.
If $f''(c)=0$, then $c$ is not a local extremum.
Every local maximum is a global maximum.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A and B**.

The critical-point definition includes both a zero derivative and a missing derivative. The second-derivative test says that a zero first derivative together with a positive second derivative produces a local minimum.

C is false because $x^{4}$ satisfies $g''(0)=0$ and has a local minimum at $0$. D is false because $x^{3}-3x$ has a local maximum value $2$ at $x=-1$ and is unbounded above.

questions.stem: The local maximum value of $f(x)=x^{3}-12x$ is an integer. Enter that integer.
questions.solution:
The answer is **16**.

$f'(x)=3x^{2}-12=3(x^{2}-4)$, so the critical points are $x=2$ and $x=-2$. The second derivative is $f''(x)=6x$. At $x=-2$, $f''(-2)=-12<0$, so this critical point is a local maximum. Its value is $f(-2)=-8-12\cdot(-2)=-8+24=16$. The other critical value is $f(2)=8-24=-16$, a local minimum.
